sec.title: Purpose of review:
sec.p: This review summarizes the latest advances in applying the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System (RTSS) to voice therapy.

sec.title: Recent findings:
sec.p: Recent RTSS work has moved beyond conceptual endorsement to practical demonstrations in vocal rehabilitation. Multiple studies now provide complete RTSS specifications of voice therapy protocols and everyday clinical care, supporting content validity and enabling direct comparison of treatment components across approaches and sites. RTSS-guided intervention development has produced componentized protocols that translate treatment theories into explicit ingredient-target hypotheses suitable for refinement through empirical testing. RTSS-based mapping has also clarified overlap and meaningful differences across evidence-based therapies. Finally, RTSS-informed evidence synthesis has reduced heterogeneity in meta-analytic work by regrouping studies according to mechanism-relevant component categories (Organ Functions vs Skills & Habits), yielding more interpretable patterns of treatment effects.

sec.title: Summary:
sec.p: The RTSS is emerging as a practical infrastructure for cumulative, component-based voice therapy science, supporting clearer intervention reporting, mechanistic interpretation, cross-disciplinary transfer, and scalable adoption in routine documentation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In the present state of treatment research, we can accumulate plenty of rigorous facts: careful empirical findings about what seems to help, in whom, and under what circumstances [1]. Behaviorally based treatment fields have rightly invested in research rigor through reforms such as clinical trial preregistration [2], improved statistical peer review [3], and reporting checklists and guidelines for manuscripts [4]. However, a collection of rigorous findings does not automatically become a usable evidence base for clinical care. To build a useful evidence base, the field also needs a shared, theory-driven framework and terminology. Without that structure, we cannot tell how findings relate, when results should generalize, or how clinicians can reliably reproduce and build on what works. In the absence of shared specification, treatments are often delivered and studied as “black box” packages [5]. When we compare packages, we may be comparing labels rather than mechanisms—without knowing whether two approaches overlap in active ingredients or differ in ways that matter.

The Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System (RTSS) was developed to provide that missing structure: a theory-driven way to describe interventions in terms of targets (the patient functions to be changed), ingredients (what clinicians do), and the hypothesized mechanisms that connect ingredients to targets [6]. The RTSS organizes treatment components into three categories: (i) Organ Functions treatments change or replace a body system (e.g., strength, range of motion, endurance, habituation to stimuli, tracheoesophageal prostheses); (ii) Skills and Habits treatments rely on learning through practice and/or feedback; and (iii) Representations treatments change knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, or other information-processing variables. A manual outlining the RTSS framework is freely available through the American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine. Van Stan and colleagues then applied the RTSS using expert-consensus Delphi methods [7] to produce an exhaustive, standardized set of unique voice therapy ingredients and targets: RTSS-Voice [8]. This review synthesizes the recent wave of RTSS-V work in vocal rehabilitation, and directly adjacent fields, to clarify what RTSS specification adds to everyday voice care. The review is organized into three sections: (1) RTSS as a bridge between voice therapy and the broader rehabilitation sciences; (2) RTSS as a tool for clarifying and strengthening the evidence base underlying vocal rehabilitation; and (3) efforts supporting RTSS adoption in real-world voice therapy.

sec.title: RTSS as a bridge between voice therapy and the broader rehabilitation sciences
sec.p: Applying the RTSS in voice therapy does more than improve treatment description; it places vocal rehabilitation inside a shared rehabilitation science framework. That shared language makes voice interventions easier to compare with—and learn from—work in motor learning, behavior change, cognition, and related domains. This need for cross-discipline treatment specification is echoed by Cochrane Rehabilitation’s Guideline for Intervention Description in rehabilitation (GUIDE-Rehab) [9], which operationalizes RTSS ideas by prompting researchers to specify targets, ingredients, dose, progression, and engagement-supporting components in a universal format. For researchers, GUIDE-Rehab helps ‘open the black box’ of rehabilitation trials by requiring a complete, RTSS-aligned specification (targets, active ingredients, dose/progression, fidelity, and comparators), which improves reproducibility and makes studies meaningfully comparable for synthesis. For clinicians, the same structure clarifies what is essential versus adaptable in an intervention, supporting consistent implementation, sensible tailoring, and clearer interpretation when outcomes fall short. Pinto and colleagues [10] and Hamilton and colleagues [11] also showed how RTSS-based treatment theories complement enablement frameworks such as the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) [12]. Treatment theory specifies how ingredients act on a specific patient function; enablement theory predicts how change in one function affects downstream functions. Used together, these frameworks connect what was delivered to why it should improve voice-related handicap, quality of life, and daily communication—exactly the kind of justification expected by health systems and payers. RTSS has increasingly been adopted across rehabilitation, but a recent scoping review [13] showed that many papers use RTSS language without producing complete specifications. Voice therapy can credibly be framed as “ahead of the curve” here because the voice literature now includes multiple published examples of full RTSS treatment specification—not just conceptual endorsement.

The RTSS’s emphasis on Skills and Habits treatment components is an immediate bridge between rehabilitation and voice therapy. Voice therapy is often primarily motor learning: patients practice new coordination patterns, learn to detect and self-correct errors, and then generalize those behaviors into real communication until they become stable under stress and cognitive load. These same skills-and-habits principles are central across dysphagia, gait, upper extremity rehabilitation, aphasia, and more—suggesting cross-disciplinary determinants of learning such as physical capacity, cognitive resources, motivation, and memory. RTSS provides a universal structure for describing Skills and Habits across this entire span, from core vocal skills (respiration, vocal function, resonance) to meta-therapeutic skills (goal planning, problem solving barriers to home practice) to non-voice skills (reaching, balance, lexical retrieval). Lyons and colleagues [14]* illustrate this transferability by creating RTSS specifications of experimental and control arms in an occupational therapy trial, showing how goal planning and problem solving can be specified as Skills/Habits components rather than vague “education.” In voice therapy, these same components address a common failure point: a patient can produce a more efficient voice in the clinic yet fail to deploy it in daily life under fatigue, stress, or time pressure. Without shared RTSS terminology, it is difficult to translate such interventions across disciplines while preserving active ingredients and links to evidence.

The RTSS also highlights how Representations treatments (i.e., teaching and learning supports) often transcend disciplinary boundaries. Turkstra and colleagues [15] recently published a cognitive rehabilitation protocol that operationalized evidence-based didactic ingredients such as elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, and teach-back. These ingredients are central to many voice interventions, where progress often depends on whether patients understand the purpose of an exercise, execute critical details of home practice, and recall strategies during a busy day. Cognitive rehabilitation has spent decades optimizing instruction when attention or memory impairments constrain uptake. While voice patients rarely present with frank cognitive impairment, the contexts where generalization must occur—high cognitive load, competing demands, stress, time pressure—can similarly undermine retention and adherence. RTSS helps the voice field borrow a mature instructional toolkit from neighboring disciplines while focusing field-specific innovation on vocal skill acquisition and habit formation.

sec.title: RTSS as a tool for clarifying and strengthening the evidence base underlying voice therapy
sec.p: RTSS specification forces any “named therapy” to be re-expressed as a set of treatment components—explicit ingredient–target pairings that are observable in routine care—rather than as an undifferentiated package. White and colleagues [16] used the RTSS to design and test the feasibility and outcomes of Pre- and Post-Operative Voice therapy for benign vocal fold lesions (PAPOV). PAPOV was deliberately decomposed into 7 essential and 4 additional components, and these components were vetted with patients and clinicians to ensure they were feasible in routine care, aligned with what clinicians already do, and tied to outcomes patients care about. Lowell and colleagues [17] used the RTSS to operationalize and refine Respiratory Lung Volume Training (RLVT) for primary muscle tension dysphonia. Experts first generated 15 candidate respiratory targets with associated ingredients based on their treatment theories. They then used structured RTSS probe questions [7] to determine which targets were truly distinct versus redundant, resulting in four unique targets with 3–7 ingredients per target. Together, PAPOV (11 components) and RLVT (4 components) provide 15 explicit hypotheses linking specific clinician actions (ingredients) to change in a single patient function (target). That structure makes component refinement straightforward: if a target does not change, or does not mediate downstream outcomes, the component can be revised. This differs from typical trials that declare primary and secondary outcomes (e.g., handicap; voice quality) without a clear statement of what about the intervention is expected to change directly versus indirectly. Once therapies are expressed in RTSS units, the evidence base is no longer tied only to fidelity to a branded protocol. Evidence can “travel” with the component. Clinicians can implement the most relevant ingredient–target pairings and document them precisely—even when real-world constraints force adaptation—while still maintaining a transparent link to what the literature actually tested.

A second benefit is that RTSS specification makes overlap and uniqueness across interventions measurable, not assumed. In our RTSS-Voice validity work [18]**, we showed that RTSS and RTSS-Voice could comprehensively specify multiple evidence-based treatments for the same diagnostic population (muscle tension dysphonia) without missing critical content. More importantly for evidence building, standardized terminology exposed commonalities and differences in targets, ingredients, and implied mechanisms across therapies—clarifying when “different schools” are truly different versus when they are variations on shared components. Two convergences were especially clear. First, all therapies addressed adherence to home practice, but they differed in the type and dose of ingredients used to support adherence. Second, nearly all therapies aimed to improve overall auditory-perceptual severity, but they pursued that target using different ingredient combinations and priorities, e.g., applying pressure to the anterior neck during voicing; resonance; airflow; exaggerated consonants/clear speech. When multiple therapies for the same diagnostic group are standardly described, network graph modeling can be applied to uncover patterns amongst targets and ingredients that may guide clinical decision making across multiple protocols, like in Fig. 1. This kind of mapping enabled the creation of Floating Ball Voice Therapy (FBVT) [19], a quantitative, virtualized treatment component that captures a treatment theory present in many evidence-based therapies for vocal hyperfunction. In FBVT, patients control a computational model of a ball floating on a column of air using vocal intensity and mean airflow to achieve a normative vocal efficiency target. Since the single outcome (vocal efficiency) can be achieved by many different airflow and intensity combinations, FBVT contains redundancy. Fig. 2 illustrates how this redundancy generates a landscape of vocal efficiency via two validated variables (airflow, intensity), and two interpretable metrics adapted from established limb motor learning research: Tolerance Cost (T-Cost) and Noise Cost (N-Cost) [20]. Both costs are quantified from data distributions (not single trial measures) and measured by their effect on the outcome of vocal efficiency. T-Cost captures systematic offsets from normative solutions; N-Cost captures the effect of the dispersion around the patient’s typical solution. Together, these metrics separate two clinically distinct improvement pathways: steering behavior towards normative solutions (Fig. 2A) versus stabilizing performance (Fig. 2B), respectively. This decomposition creates a direct bridge from motor learning science to voice rehabilitation, yielding mechanistic markers of how individual patients improve performance, not merely whether or not a patient improves. More broadly, RTSS mapping supports a next step that voice therapy needs: taking implicit treatment theories and turning them into measurable, testable components—often in forms that can scale as digital therapeutics while preserving essential active ingredients.

Finally, RTSS specification improves evidence synthesis because meta-analyses are only as interpretable as the treatment descriptions they pool. Saccente-Kennedy and colleagues [21] conducted a meta-analysis of presbyphonia treatments, first using the conventional approach of pooling all interventions together, and then regrouping interventions using RTSS component categories (Organ Functions, Skills and Habits, Representations). When all therapies were pooled, heterogeneity was high—an expected result when studies with different targets and ingredients are treated as interchangeable simply because they share the label “voice therapy.” Regrouping by RTSS categories reduced heterogeneity by comparing more similar interventions. Across studies, they found convincing overall benefit of voice therapy on patient-reported outcomes and physiologic/acoustic measures. But they also found a clinically meaningful pattern: Organ Functions–dominant approaches produced larger gains in maximum phonation time (MPT) than Skills & Habits–dominant approaches. This is the type of inference conventional reviews often cannot support because treatment content is under-described. RTSS-based regrouping did more than improve statistics; it linked effects to treatment logic. A larger MPT gain under Organ Functions–dominant protocols is plausible if those protocols more directly target physiologic capacity, tissue-level function, or glottal valving. Skills & Habits–dominant protocols may instead prioritize coordination, efficiency, and generalization into real communication—outcomes that may not be best captured by MPT alone. This framing makes it easier to be explicit about which outcomes are proximal versus downstream for a given target class. It also sets up sharper next steps: comparative presbyphonia trials can intentionally balance Organ Functions and Skills & Habits targets (and, when relevant, Representations targets such as knowledge and adherence), track component dose and fidelity, and test a priori hypotheses about which target classes most strongly drive which outcomes.

sec.title: Efforts supporting adoption of the RTSS in standard of care voice therapy
sec.p: Gibson and colleagues [22]* provide a practical blueprint for RTSS adoption that is directly portable to voice clinics: a structured program that trains clinicians to specify treatment components (targets, ingredients, and mechanisms) and then use that language in routine documentation. In an acute inpatient physiotherapy setting, 26 physiotherapists completed short didactic teaching, case-based learning, an introductory e-learning module, and—most importantly—documentation workshops focused on translating RTSS thinking into everyday notes. After training, clinicians used RTSS controlled-vocabulary terms more often in case notes and reported improved clinical reasoning that persisted at two months. The blunt takeaway for voice settings is that RTSS adoption is not a “read the framework” problem. It is a workflow training problem: teach it, practice it on real cases, and rehearse how to document it in the local note template while explicitly addressing barriers that affect uptake.

Complementing that implementation work, Wolfberg and colleagues [23]** demonstrated how RTSS-Voice documentation can convert routine clinical care into analyzable treatment data. Unlike evaluation reports—which often follow stable templates and shared reporting conventions—standard-of-care voice therapy notes are rarely standardized. Many clinicians use a SOAP shell, but the content is narrative and idiosyncratic across clinicians and sites, making it hard to compare what “standard care” actually contains. In their multisite study, five experienced voice SLPs from five centers recorded 59 therapy sessions; all were specifiable using RTSS and RTSS-Voice without adding new targets or ingredients—supporting content validity in everyday care. Several commonalities emerged across sites: volition (adherence/engagement) was present in all sessions; decreased strained voice quality was a dominant target in nearly all sessions; volition ingredients oriented towards the patient’s capability and motivation to practice at home were ubiquitous; feedback was nearly universal and was largely knowledge-of-results; and practice opportunities nearly always emphasized mean airflow, resonance, and pitch variability. At the same time, RTSS-Voice revealed meaningful differences between clinicians: some primarily delivered two components (home practice adherence and reduced strain), whereas others often added a variety of treatment components (e.g., reduced muscle activation level; improved abdominal movement; education). For adoption efforts, this is the payoff: RTSS-Voice documentation does not just make notes cleaner—it makes clinical care comparable across clinicians and centers and supports quality improvement and cumulative evidence generation about what “standard care” actually is.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Recent RTSS-Voice work has pushed treatment specification from a promising idea to usable tools and real-world demonstrations in vocal rehabilitation. New studies show that RTSS mapping can (i) design and refine componentized protocols (e.g., PAPOV; RLVT), (ii) reveal shared and differentiating treatment theories across evidence-based approaches and across clinics, (iii) improve meta-analytic interpretability by grouping interventions by mechanism-relevant content, and (iv) connect voice therapy more directly to broader rehabilitation science. Early implementation results suggest RTSS language can also be taught and adopted in routine documentation, supporting a cumulative, component-based evidence base for voice therapy.

caption.p: Directed, annotated network graph based on RTSS specifications for Vocal Function Exercises (blue), Conversation Training Therapy (red), Laryngeal Reposturing (Gray), and Circumlaryngeal Massage (green). Each node (circle) represents a single target and the edge connections (arrows) show clinical decision-making paths across and within protocols. For example, Vocal Function Exercises asks patients to adhere to three Skills and Habits targets in hopes that they will improve overall auditory perceptual severity. In contrast, the other three protocols start at targeting auditory perceptual severity and branch out to other targets based on the patient’s response. All 4 protocols used adherence in daily life to further habituate improvements in auditory perceptual severity, with Circumlaryngeal Massage and Laryngeal Reposturing using education in hopes of indirectly maximizing adherence.

Floating Ball Therapy’s landscape in 3 dimensions with airflow (x-axis), intensity (z-axis), error (y-axis, black-yellow-white color). Highest possible error represented by peaks on the left/farther (pressed voicing: low flow per intensity) and right/closer (breathy voicing: high flow per intensity). Each panel shows a single sustained vowel trial (set of grey circles) and optimized data sets for T-Cost (red circles) and N-Cost (blue circles). (A) An example trial where shifting the data and improving tolerance is most beneficial, i.e. exploration in early practice affords more improvement that reducing noise. (B) An example trial where reducing noise affords more improvement that increasing tolerance; i.e., channeling variability affords more improvement than gross exploration. The amount of improvement is quantified by T-cost and N-cost.

boxed-text.p: Voice therapy is increasingly legible within the broader rehabilitation sciences: RTSS-Voice clarifies how core voice therapy principles (motor learning; practice/feedback; adherence/volition; teaching/Representations) overlap with and can borrow from PT/OT, aphasia, cognitive rehabilitation, and behavior change.

RTSS-Voice has shifted from concept to practice: multiple recent papers provide complete RTSS/RTSS-Voice specifications of real-world voice therapy, improving reproducibility and comparison across studies.

RTSS-guided protocol development provides a replicable playbook for turning treatment theories into feasible, componentized interventions with explicit ingredient–target hypotheses (e.g., PAPOV; RLVT).

Cross-protocol and cross-clinic mapping is exposing a “common core” of care (e.g., adherence support; reduced strain aims) alongside meaningful differences in targets, ingredients, and prioritization across clinicians and sites.

RTSS is improving evidence synthesis: RTSS-based regrouping in meta-analysis reduces heterogeneity and yields theory-relevant treatment effect patterns (e.g., Organ Functions vs Skills & Habits differences in presbyphonia outcomes).

**Van Stan et al., 2024 provide RTSS specifications of Circumlaryngeal Massage, Conversation Training Therapy, Laryngeal Reposturing, and Vocal Function Exercises that have been approved by both interdisciplinary RTSS experts and the protocol developers. The supplementary materials provide the entire specifications.

**Wolfberg et al., 2024 provide RTSS specifications of nearly 50 standard of care therapy sessions across five clinicians from different voice centers. The supplemental materials provide examples of using the RTSS in standard of care documentation for all sessions.

*Lyons et al, 2024 provide RTSS specifications of skills and habits treatments with direct applicability to voice therapy: improve problem solving, improve goal setting, improve use of action plans in daily life. They also specify general therapist factors associated with creating an empathetic therapeutic interaction.

*Gibson et al., 2025 provide a training program to help front line clinicians apply the RTSS in their clinical reasoning and documentation. It also demonstrated success for improved clinical reasoning and increased use of RTSS terms in documentation.
